item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=information+gain+autonomous+agents+task+decomposition+principles&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7654458\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Information Gain--Convergence Costs, Hesitation Guidance, and Auditable Task Progress in LLM Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p><span>Response speed, information acquisition, and task advancement are distinct properties of LLM agents. This paper separates observational novelty, obligation evidence, and contract-relevant artifact changes through a retrospective study of RHIS records. This spans early model comparisons (GLM vs. DeepSeek), the development and runtime verification of hesitation guidance (V105), and a six-domain R12 run. In a paired comparison with the same checkpoint and public task, DeepSeek V4 Pro achieved an 865/964 official check pass rate in 30.37% of the wall-clock time used by GLM-5.3. This end-to-end efficiency result does not, however, estimate a guidance effect. The V105 Code trace records a guidance trigger entering the archived request, followed by autonomous model actions, readback, and a 17/17 pass. In R12 (88 HTTP requests, 109 hesitation-frontier observations), all observations were flagged as novel, yet no hesitation direction was triggered; a separate production-progress diagnostic delivered feedback across five domains. In the Web domain, no required-artifact advancement was witnessed for the first fourteen actions, despite continuous novel returns. Feedback was queued after action three and delivered after action nine, with verified artifacts appearing at actions fifteen through seventeen. These records establish both an operational guidance mechanism and a coverage boundary of novelty-based monitoring. While \\\"pseudo-productivity\\\" remains a diagnostic hypothesis requiring task-relevance review, the evidence demonstrates that observational novelty is not a sufficient condition for task progress. Causal benefits of guidance still require controlled comparisons.</span></p>\\n<br></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7654458\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/gats7678\", \"title\": [\"Decentralized coordination via task de…

Causal benefits of guidance still require controlled comparisons.</span></p>\\n<br></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7654458\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/gats7678\", \"title\": [\"Decentralized coordination via task decomposition and reward shaping\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>In this work, we introduce a method for decentralized coordination in cooperative multiagent multi-task problems where the subtasks and agents are homogeneous. Using the method proposed, the agents cooperate at the high level task selection using the knowledge they gather by learning subtasks. We introduce a subtask selection method for single agent multi-task MDPs and we extend the work to multiagent multi-task MDPs by using reward shaping at the subtask level to coordinate the agents. Our results on a multi-rover problem show that agents which use the combination of task decomposition and subtask based difference rewards result in significant improvement both in terms of learning speed, and converged policies.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/gats7678\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 5, 6]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/jrtr4235\", \"title\": [\"Transferring experience in reinforcement learning through task decomposition\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Transfer learning refers to the process of conveying experience from a simple task to another more complex (and related) task in order to reduce the amount of time that is required to learn the latter task. Typically, in a transfer learning procedure the agent learns a behavior in a source task, and it uses the gained knowledge in order to speed up the learning process in a target task. Reinforcement Learning algorithms are time expensive when they learn from scratch, especially in complex domains, and transfer learning comprises a suitable solution to speed up the training process. In this work we propose a method that decomposes the target task in several instances of the source task and uses them to extract an advised action for the target task. We evaluate the efficacy of the proposed approach in the robotic soccer Keepaway domain. The results demonstrate that the proposed method helps to reduce the training time of the target task.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/jrtr4235\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 5, 10]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/ybhp5862\", \"title\": [\"Automatic task decomposition and state abstraction from demonstration\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Both Learning from Demonstration (LfD) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) are popular approaches for building decision-making agents. LfD applies supervised learning to a set of human demonstrations to infer and imitate the human policy, while RL uses only a reward signal and exploration to find an optimal policy. For complex tasks both of these techniques may be ineffective. LfD may require many more demonstrations than it is feasible to obtain, and RL can take an inadmissible amount of time to converge. We present Automatic Decomposition and Abstraction from demonstration (ADA), an algorithm that uses mutual information measures over a set of human demonstrations to decompose a sequential decision process into several subtasks, finding state abstractions for each one of these subtasks. ADA then projects the human demonstrations into the abstracted state space to build a policy. This policy can later be improved using RL algorithms to surpass the performance of the human teacher. We find empirically that ADA can find satisficing policies for problems that are too complex to be solved with traditional LfD and RL algorithms. In particular, we show that we can use mutual information across state features to leverage human demonstrations to reduce the effects of the curse of dimensionality by finding subtasks and abstractions in sequential decision processes.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/ybhp5862\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2012, 6, 4]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "87701b0c7987e7c0c3dbf9a2fc14e96e636f14901d9eb494e0aa5380ade586b6", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_inquiry", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7654458", "doi:10.65109/gats7678", "doi:10.65109/jrtr4235", "doi:10.65109/ybhp5862"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7654458", "https://doi.org/10.65109/gats7678", "https://doi.org/10.65109/jrtr4235", "https://doi.org/10.65109/ybhp5862"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
